sections.title: Atomic structure and the periodic table

paras.text: The periodic table provides chemists with a structured organisation of the known chemical elements from which they can make sense of their physical and chemical properties. The historical development of the periodic table and models of atomic structure provide good examples of how scientific ideas and explanations develop over time as new evidence emerges. The arrangement of elements in the modern periodic table can be explained in terms of atomic structure which provides evidence for the model of a nuclear atom with electrons in energy levels.

sections.title: A simple model of the atom, symbols, relative atomic mass, electronic charge and isotopes

paras.text: All substances are made of atoms. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
Atoms of each element are represented by a chemical symbol, eg O represents an atom of oxygen, Na represents an atom of sodium.
There are about 100 different elements. Elements are shown in the periodic table.

Compounds are formed from elements by chemical reactions. Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances, and often involve a detectable energy change. Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions and can be represented by formulae using the symbols of the atoms from which they were formed. Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.
Chemical reactions can be represented by word equations or equations using symbols and formulae.

Students will be supplied with a periodic table for the exam and should be able to: • use the names and symbols of the first 20 elements in the periodic table, the elements in Groups 1 and 7, and other elements in this specification • name compounds of these elements from given formulae or symbol equations • write word equations for the reactions in this specification • write formulae and balanced chemical equations for the reactions in this specification.
(HT only) write balanced half equations and ionic equations where appropriate.

los.t: Define an atom and state that all substances are made of atoms

k.t: All substances are made of atoms. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can exist.
An element contains only one type of atom (all atoms with the same number of protons).

los.t: Represent atoms of elements using chemical symbols

k.t: Atoms of each element are represented by a chemical symbol, eg O represents an atom of oxygen, Na represents an atom of sodium.
Symbols have one capital letter followed (if there is a second letter) by a lower-case letter: Co (cobalt) is an element, CO (carbon monoxide) is a compound.

los.t: State how many elements there are and where they are shown

k.t: There are about 100 different elements. Elements are shown in the periodic table.

los.t: Describe how compounds are formed and what chemical reactions involve

k.t: Compounds are formed from elements by chemical reactions.
Chemical reactions always involve the formation of one or more new substances, and often involve a detectable energy change.
Detectable energy change = temperature rise or fall, light given out, etc.

los.t: Define a compound and state how it can be represented and separated

k.t: Compounds contain two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions.
Compounds can be represented by formulae using the symbols of the atoms from which they were formed.
Compounds can only be separated into elements by chemical reactions.

Compound vs mixture: compounds have fixed proportions, properties different from the elements, separated only by chemical reactions; mixtures have variable composition and are separated by physical processes (see 4.1.1.2).

los.t: Represent chemical reactions as word equations and symbol equations

k.t: Chemical reactions can be represented by word equations or equations using symbols and formulae.
Word equation example: magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide. Symbol equation: 2Mg + O2 → 2MgO.

los.t: Use names and symbols of the first 20 elements, Group 1 and Group 7 elements and other elements in the specification

k.t: Students will be supplied with a periodic table for the exam.
Use the names and symbols of the first 20 elements in the periodic table, the elements in Groups 1 and 7, and other elements in this specification.
First 20: H, He, Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, Ne, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar, K, Ca. Group 1: Li, Na, K (Rb, Cs, Fr below). Group 7: F, Cl, Br, I (At).

Other elements named in this specification include Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, Au, Pb, Sn, Ti, Cr, Mn, Co, Ni, Pt, Ba, Sr, Hg and others met in later topics – check each topic's list. The periodic table is supplied but you must know symbols without a data table for the first 20 so you can use them fluently.

los.t: Name compounds from given formulae or symbol equations

k.t: Name compounds of these elements from given formulae or symbol equations.

Rules: metal first then non-metal ending -ide (NaCl sodium chloride); -ate means oxygen present with another element (CuSO4 copper sulfate; CaCO3 calcium carbonate); -ite has less oxygen; hydroxide = OH; hydrogencarbonate etc. as met later.

los.t: Write word equations for the reactions in the specification

k.t: Write word equations for the reactions in this specification.

los.t: Write formulae and balanced symbol equations for the reactions in the specification

k.t: Write formulae and balanced chemical equations for the reactions in this specification.
Balancing: write correct formulae FIRST (never change subscripts), then adjust big numbers in front until each element has the same number of atoms on both sides.

los.t: Write balanced half equations and ionic equations where appropriate

k.t: (HT only) write balanced half equations and ionic equations where appropriate.
Ionic equation: cancel spectator ions; balance atoms AND charge. Half equation: show electron transfer (oxidation loses e–, reduction gains e–). Examples: Ag+ + Cl– → AgCl; 2Br– → Br2 + 2e–.

paras.text: A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together. The chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.
notes: Safe use of a range of equipment to separate chemical mixtures.

paras.text: Mixtures can be separated by physical processes such as filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography. These physical processes do not involve chemical reactions and no new substances are made.

Students should be able to: • describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation • suggest suitable separation and purification techniques for mixtures when given appropriate information.

los.t: Define a mixture

k.t: A mixture consists of two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together.
The chemical properties of each substance in the mixture are unchanged.
Air (N2, O2, Ar, CO2…), sea water, alloys, crude oil.

los.t: Name the physical processes that separate mixtures and state that no new substances are made

k.t: Mixtures can be separated by physical processes such as filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography.
These physical processes do not involve chemical reactions and no new substances are made.

los.t: Describe, explain and give examples of filtration

k.t: Describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation (filtration).
Pour mixture through filter paper in a funnel; insoluble solid (residue) stays on the paper; solution/liquid (filtrate) passes through.
Separating sand from water; removing excess insoluble solid (e.g. copper oxide) from a salt solution.
Works because insoluble particles are too large to pass through the tiny holes in filter paper but dissolved particles/liquid particles are small enough.

los.t: Describe, explain and give examples of crystallisation

k.t: Describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation (crystallisation).

Heat solution to evaporate some water until saturated (crystals appear on a glass rod dipped in); leave to cool slowly; crystals form; filter, wash with a little cold distilled water, dry between filter paper.
Obtaining copper sulfate crystals from copper sulfate solution; obtaining salt from salt solution (evaporation to dryness if the solid does not decompose).
Solubility of the dissolved solid decreases as the solution cools, so excess solute comes out as crystals.

los.t: Describe, explain and give examples of simple distillation

k.t: Describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation (simple distillation).
Heat solution; solvent evaporates; vapour passes through a condenser (cold water in at the bottom, out at the top); pure liquid collects as distillate; dissolved solid stays behind.
Obtaining pure water from salt water.
Works because the solvent has a much lower boiling point than the dissolved solid.

los.t: Describe, explain and give examples of fractional distillation

k.t: Describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation (fractional distillation).

Mixture of liquids heated in a flask; vapours rise up a fractionating column (temperature gradient – hotter at the bottom, cooler at the top); the lowest boiling point component reaches the top first and is condensed and collected; others condense lower down or remain.
Separating ethanol from water; separating crude oil into fractions (4.7.1.2); separating liquefied air gases.
Works because components have different boiling points.

los.t: Describe, explain and give examples of chromatography

k.t: Describe, explain and give examples of the specified processes of separation (chromatography).

Draw a pencil baseline; spot samples on it; place paper in solvent with the baseline ABOVE the solvent level; solvent travels up carrying substances; remove before solvent reaches the top and mark the solvent front. Full detail and Rf values in 4.8.1 and Required practical 6.
Substances separate because they differ in solubility in the solvent (mobile phase) and attraction to the paper (stationary phase).

los.t: Suggest suitable separation and purification techniques for mixtures when given appropriate information

k.t: Suggest suitable separation and purification techniques for mixtures when given appropriate information.

Decision guide: insoluble solid + liquid → filtration; soluble solid wanted from solution → crystallisation; liquid solvent wanted from solution → simple distillation; miscible liquids with different boiling points → fractional distillation; several dissolved coloured substances → chromatography. Look for the properties given (solubility, boiling point, state).
Safe use of a range of equipment to separate chemical mixtures (AT 4) and the WS 2.2, 2.3 skills attached to this section: carry out experiments safely and make/record observations.

sections.title: The development of the model of the atom (common content with physics)

paras.text: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
notes: WS 1.1, 1.6 This historical context provides an opportunity for students to show an understanding of why and describe how scientific methods and theories develop over time.

paras.text: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom. The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.

The results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged. This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances. The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.

Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge. The name proton was given to these particles.
The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus. This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Students should be able to describe: • why the new evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model
• the difference between the plum pudding model of the atom and the nuclear model of the atom.
Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
Details of Chadwick’s experimental work are not required.

los.t: State that new evidence may change or replace a scientific model

k.t: New experimental evidence may lead to a scientific model being changed or replaced.
WS 1.1, 1.6 – this historical context provides an opportunity for students to show an understanding of why and describe how scientific methods and theories develop over time.
A model is accepted only while it explains all the evidence; when new, reliable, repeatable evidence contradicts it, the model is modified or replaced.

los.t: Describe the early 'solid sphere' model of the atom

k.t: Before the discovery of the electron, atoms were thought to be tiny spheres that could not be divided.
Dalton's model: atoms of each element are identical solid spheres (indivisible).

los.t: Describe the plum pudding model and what led to it

k.t: The discovery of the electron led to the plum pudding model of the atom.
The plum pudding model suggested that the atom is a ball of positive charge with negative electrons embedded in it.
The electron was discovered by J. J. Thomson. Overall the atom is neutral because positive charge balances the negative electrons.

los.t: Explain how the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the nuclear model

k.t: The results from the alpha particle scattering experiment led to the conclusion that the mass of an atom was concentrated at the centre (nucleus) and that the nucleus was charged.
This nuclear model replaced the plum pudding model.
WS 1.2 (use of models).

Expected result for plum pudding: alpha particles pass straight through or are slightly deflected. Observed (Geiger–Marsden under Rutherford): most passed straight through (atom is mostly empty space); a small number were deflected through large angles and a very few bounced back (nucleus is small, dense, positively charged, containing most of the mass).
Names of scientists and fine details of the experiment are not named in the specification wording for this point; know the observations and conclusions.

los.t: Describe Bohr's adaptation of the nuclear model

k.t: Niels Bohr adapted the nuclear model by suggesting that electrons orbit the nucleus at specific distances.
The theoretical calculations of Bohr agreed with experimental observations.
Details of experimental work supporting the Bohr model are not required.
This is the origin of electron shells/energy levels (4.1.1.7). Orbits at fixed distances stop electrons spiralling into the nucleus.

los.t: Describe how the proton was identified

k.t: Later experiments led to the idea that the positive charge of any nucleus could be subdivided into a whole number of smaller particles, each particle having the same amount of positive charge.
The name proton was given to these particles.

los.t: Describe the evidence for neutrons and its timing

k.t: The experimental work of James Chadwick provided the evidence to show the existence of neutrons within the nucleus.
This was about 20 years after the nucleus became an accepted scientific idea.
Details of Chadwick's experimental work are not required.

los.t: Describe why scattering evidence led to a change in the atomic model

k.t: Students should be able to describe why the new evidence from the scattering experiment led to a change in the atomic model.
Structure the answer: expected result under the old model → actual observation → what that shows about the atom → new model.

los.t: Describe the difference between the plum pudding and nuclear models

k.t: Students should be able to describe the difference between the plum pudding model of the atom and the nuclear model of the atom.
Plum pudding: positive charge spread evenly through a ball with electrons embedded. Nuclear: tiny dense positively charged nucleus with most of the mass, electrons surrounding it, mostly empty space.

los.t: Order the models of the atom historically

k.t: Sequence implied by the specification statements: solid sphere → plum pudding → nuclear → Bohr → protons → neutrons.
Useful for 'describe how the model has changed' questions.

sections.title: Relative electrical charges of subatomic particles

paras.text: The relative electrical charges of the particles in atoms are: [Table in specification — Name of particle / Relative charge: Proton +1; Neutron 0; Electron –1]
In an atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. Atoms have no overall electrical charge.
The number of protons in an atom of an element is its atomic number. All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons. Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.
Students should be able to use the nuclear model to describe atoms.

los.t: State the relative charges of protons, neutrons and electrons

k.t: The relative electrical charges of the particles in atoms are: proton +1, neutron 0, electron –1 (table in specification).
Relative charge – compared with the proton; not an absolute charge in coulombs.

los.t: State that atoms are neutral and why

k.t: In an atom, the number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in the nucleus. Atoms have no overall electrical charge.

los.t: Define atomic number and apply it to elements

k.t: The number of protons in an atom of an element is its atomic number.
All atoms of a particular element have the same number of protons.
Atoms of different elements have different numbers of protons.
The atomic number identifies the element. Changing the number of neutrons gives an isotope; changing the number of protons gives a different element.

los.t: Use the nuclear model to describe atoms

k.t: Students should be able to use the nuclear model to describe atoms (WS 1.2).
Tiny central nucleus containing protons and neutrons; electrons in shells around it; most of the atom is empty space.
Be able to draw a labelled nuclear-model diagram of a simple atom (e.g. lithium: 3 protons and 4 neutrons in nucleus; electrons 2,1).

paras.text: Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
notes: WS 4.3, 4.4 Use SI units and the prefix nano.

paras.text: The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom (about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m).
notes: MS 1b Recognise expressions in standard form.

paras.text: Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
The relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons are: [Table in specification — Name of particle / Relative mass: Proton 1; Neutron 1; Electron Very small]
The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom is its mass number.
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
Atoms can be represented as shown in this example: [Figure in specification — sodium written as ²³₁₁Na with 23 labelled 'Mass number' and 11 labelled 'Atomic number']
Students should be able to calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion, given its atomic number and mass number.
Students should be able to relate size and scale of atoms to objects in the physical world.

los.t: State the size of an atom and use nano units

k.t: Atoms are very small, having a radius of about 0.1 nm (1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m).
Use SI units and the prefix nano (WS 4.3, 4.4).

los.t: State the size of the nucleus relative to the atom

k.t: The radius of a nucleus is less than 1/10 000 of that of the atom (about 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ m).
Recognise expressions in standard form (MS 1b).
Atom radius ÷ nucleus radius ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ ÷ 1 × 10⁻¹⁴ = 10 000 (so the nucleus is 1/10 000 of the radius).

los.t: State where most of the mass of an atom is

k.t: Almost all of the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.

los.t: State the relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons

k.t: The relative masses are: proton 1, neutron 1, electron very small (table in specification).
Do NOT write 0 for an electron's mass; use 'very small' (about 1/1835 of a proton).

los.t: Define mass number

k.t: The sum of the protons and neutrons in an atom is its mass number.

los.t: Define isotopes

k.t: Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons; these atoms are called isotopes of that element.
Same number of protons (same element, same chemical properties) but different numbers of neutrons (different mass number).
Carbon-12 and carbon-14: both 6 protons; 6 vs 8 neutrons. Chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.

los.t: Read and write nuclear symbols showing mass number and atomic number

k.t: Atoms can be represented as shown in this example: ²³₁₁Na with mass number (23) as the upper number and atomic number (11) as the lower number (figure in specification).
Top = mass number (bigger); bottom = atomic number (smaller, identifies the element).

los.t: Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion

k.t: Calculate the numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in an atom or ion, given its atomic number and mass number (MS 1d).
protons = atomic number; neutrons = mass number – atomic number; electrons = protons (atom) ± charge for an ion (positive ion: lose electrons; negative ion: gain electrons).
Example: ²⁷₁₃Al³⁺ → 13 protons, 14 neutrons, 10 electrons. ³⁵₁₇Cl⁻ → 17 protons, 18 neutrons, 18 electrons.

los.t: Relate the size and scale of atoms to objects in the physical world

k.t: Students should be able to relate size and scale of atoms to objects in the physical world.
Atom ≈ 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m; small molecule ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁹ m; nanoparticle 1–100 nm; cell ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁵ m; thickness of a human hair ≈ 1 × 10⁻⁴ m. Compare using standard form and orders of magnitude.

paras.text: The relative atomic mass of an element is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.
Students should be able to calculate the relative atomic mass of an element given the percentage abundance of its isotopes.

los.t: Define relative atomic mass as an average accounting for isotope abundance

k.t: The relative atomic mass of an element is an average value that takes account of the abundance of the isotopes of the element.
This is why relative atomic masses (Ar) are often not whole numbers, e.g. chlorine 35.5.

los.t: Calculate the relative atomic mass of an element from isotope percentage abundances

k.t: Students should be able to calculate the relative atomic mass of an element given the percentage abundance of its isotopes.
Ar = (isotope mass × % abundance of that isotope + other isotope mass × % …) ÷ 100.
Check the answer lies between the lightest and heaviest isotope and closer to the more abundant one.

paras.text: The electrons in an atom occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells). The electronic structure of an atom can be represented by numbers or by a diagram. For example, the electronic structure of sodium is 2,8,1 or [Figure in specification — concentric-circle diagram, sodium: 2 electrons in first shell, 8 in second, 1 in third] showing two electrons in the lowest energy level, eight in the second energy level and one in the third energy level.
Students should be able to represent the electronic structures of the first twenty elements of the periodic table in both forms.
notes: MS 5b Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects.

paras.text: Students may answer questions in terms of either energy levels or shells.

los.t: State that electrons occupy the lowest available energy levels first

k.t: The electrons in an atom occupy the lowest available energy levels (innermost available shells).

los.t: Represent electronic structure by numbers and by diagram

k.t: The electronic structure of an atom can be represented by numbers or by a diagram.

For example, the electronic structure of sodium is 2,8,1 or (concentric-circle diagram) showing two electrons in the lowest energy level, eight in the second energy level and one in the third energy level.
Diagram: nucleus at the centre with concentric circles; dots/crosses on each circle for electrons.

los.t: Write the electronic structures of the first 20 elements in both forms

k.t: Students should be able to represent the electronic structures of the first twenty elements of the periodic table in both forms.
Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects (MS 5b).
Filling rule: max 2 in first shell, 8 in second, 8 in third (up to calcium: 2,8,8,2). Examples: Li 2,1; C 2,4; O 2,6; Na 2,8,1; Cl 2,8,7; K 2,8,8,1; Ca 2,8,8,2.
Group number = number of outer-shell electrons (Groups 1–7, Group 0 full); period number = number of shells.

los.t: Answer questions in terms of energy levels or shells

k.t: Students may answer questions in terms of either energy levels or shells.

paras.text: The elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number and so that elements with similar properties are in columns, known as groups. The table is called a periodic table because similar properties occur at regular intervals.
Elements in the same group in the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (outer electrons) and this gives them similar chemical properties.

Students should be able to: • explain how the position of an element in the periodic table is related to the arrangement of electrons in its atoms and hence to its atomic number • predict possible reactions and probable reactivity of elements from their positions in the periodic table.

los.t: Describe how elements are arranged in the periodic table

k.t: The elements in the periodic table are arranged in order of atomic (proton) number and so that elements with similar properties are in columns, known as groups.

los.t: Explain why it is called a periodic table

k.t: The table is called a periodic table because similar properties occur at regular intervals.

los.t: Relate group to outer electrons and similar chemical properties

k.t: Elements in the same group in the periodic table have the same number of electrons in their outer shell (outer electrons) and this gives them similar chemical properties.

los.t: Explain how an element's position relates to its electron arrangement and atomic number

k.t: Explain how the position of an element in the periodic table is related to the arrangement of electrons in its atoms and hence to its atomic number.
Link: atomic number → electron arrangement (e.g. 2,8,7) → group (7) and period (3) → position → chemical properties.

los.t: Predict reactions and reactivity from position in the periodic table

k.t: Predict possible reactions and probable reactivity of elements from their positions in the periodic table.
Use group trends (4.1.2.4–4.1.2.6 and 4.4.1) and the metal/non-metal division.

paras.text: Before the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.
notes: WS 1.1, 1.6 Explain how testing a prediction can support or refute a new scientific idea.

paras.text: The early periodic tables were incomplete and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed.
Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements that he thought had not been discovered and in some places changed the order based on atomic weights.
Elements with properties predicted by Mendeleev were discovered and filled the gaps. Knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.
Students should be able to describe these steps in the development of the periodic table.

los.t: Describe early classification by atomic weight

k.t: Before the discovery of protons, neutrons and electrons, scientists attempted to classify the elements by arranging them in order of their atomic weights.
WS 1.1, 1.6 – explain how testing a prediction can support or refute a new scientific idea.

los.t: Describe the problems with early periodic tables

k.t: The early periodic tables were incomplete and some elements were placed in inappropriate groups if the strict order of atomic weights was followed.

los.t: Describe how Mendeleev overcame the problems

k.t: Mendeleev overcame some of the problems by leaving gaps for elements that he thought had not been discovered and in some places changed the order based on atomic weights.
Leaving gaps made predictions about undiscovered elements' properties; swapping order kept elements with similar properties in the same group (e.g. tellurium and iodine).

los.t: Explain how predictions were tested and why order by atomic weight was sometimes wrong

k.t: Elements with properties predicted by Mendeleev were discovered and filled the gaps.
Knowledge of isotopes made it possible to explain why the order based on atomic weights was not always correct.
Successful predictions (e.g. germanium) supported his table. Average atomic weight depends on isotope abundance, whereas the real order is by number of protons.

los.t: Describe the steps in the development of the periodic table

k.t: Students should be able to describe these steps in the development of the periodic table.
Sequence: order by atomic weight → problems → Mendeleev gaps and swaps → predictions confirmed → isotopes explain the anomalies → order by atomic number.

paras.text: Elements that react to form positive ions are metals.
Elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.
The majority of elements are metals. Metals are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table. Non-metals are found towards the right and top of the periodic table.

Students should be able to: • explain the differences between metals and non-metals on the basis of their characteristic physical and chemical properties. This links to Group 0 (page 24), Group 1 (page 24), Group 7 (page 25) and Bonding, structure and the properties of matter (page 26) • explain how the atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their position in the periodic table • explain how the reactions of elements are related to the arrangement of electrons in their atoms and hence to their atomic number.

los.t: Define metals and non-metals by ion formation

k.t: Elements that react to form positive ions are metals.
Elements that do not form positive ions are non-metals.

los.t: State the proportion and position of metals and non-metals in the periodic table

k.t: The majority of elements are metals.
Metals are found to the left and towards the bottom of the periodic table.
Non-metals are found towards the right and top of the periodic table.

los.t: Explain differences between metals and non-metals using physical and chemical properties

k.t: Explain the differences between metals and non-metals on the basis of their characteristic physical and chemical properties.
This links to Group 0 (page 24), Group 1 (page 24), Group 7 (page 25) and Bonding, structure and the properties of matter (page 26).

Metals: conduct heat and electricity, malleable/ductile, shiny, high melting/boiling points (generally), form basic oxides, form positive ions. Non-metals: poor conductors (graphite/graphene exceptions), brittle when solid, dull, low melting/boiling points (generally, except giant covalent), form acidic oxides, do not form positive ions.

los.t: Explain how atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their position

k.t: Explain how the atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their position in the periodic table.
Metals have few outer electrons (1–3) which they lose easily to form positive ions; non-metals have more outer electrons (4–7) and tend to gain or share them.

los.t: Explain how reactions of elements relate to electron arrangement and atomic number

k.t: Explain how the reactions of elements are related to the arrangement of electrons in their atoms and hence to their atomic number.

paras.text: The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table are called the noble gases. They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons. The noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell, except for helium, which has only two electrons.
The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass (going down the group).
Students should be able to: • explain how properties of the elements in Group 0 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms • predict properties from given trends down the group.

los.t: Name Group 0 and state why the noble gases are unreactive

k.t: The elements in Group 0 of the periodic table are called the noble gases.
They are unreactive and do not easily form molecules because their atoms have stable arrangements of electrons.

los.t: State the number of outer electrons in noble gases

k.t: The noble gases have eight electrons in their outer shell, except for helium, which has only two electrons.

los.t: State the trend in boiling point down Group 0

k.t: The boiling points of the noble gases increase with increasing relative atomic mass (going down the group).
Helium –269 °C, neon –246 °C, argon –186 °C, krypton –153 °C, xenon –108 °C (illustrative data).

los.t: Explain how Group 0 properties depend on the outer shell of electrons

k.t: Explain how properties of the elements in Group 0 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms.
Full outer shell → no need to lose, gain or share electrons → unreactive, monatomic gases.

los.t: Predict properties from given trends down the group

k.t: Predict properties from given trends down the group.
Interpolate/extrapolate from the data: e.g. estimate the boiling point of an element between two others in the group.

paras.text: The elements in Group 1 of the periodic table are known as the alkali metals and have characteristic properties because of the single electron in their outer shell.
Students should be able to describe the reactions of the first three alkali metals with oxygen, chlorine and water.
In Group 1, the reactivity of the elements increases going down the group.
Students should be able to: • explain how properties of the elements in Group 1 depend on the outer shell of electrons of the atoms • predict properties from given trends down the group.

los.t: Name Group 1 and link its properties to one outer electron

los.t: Describe the reactions of Li, Na and K with oxygen, chlorine and water

Group 1 properties: soft, low density (Li, Na, K float on water), low melting points; these trends: melting point decreases down the group.

sections.title: Bonding, structure, and the properties of matter

paras.text: Chemists use theories of structure and bonding to explain the physical and chemical properties of materials. Analysis of structures shows that atoms can be arranged in a variety of ways, some of which are molecular while others are giant structures. Theories of bonding explain how atoms are held together in these structures. Scientists use this knowledge of structure and bonding to engineer new materials with desirable properties. The properties of these materials may offer new applications in a range of different technologies.

sections.title: Chemical bonds, ionic, covalent and metallic

paras.text: There are three types of strong chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic. For ionic bonding the particles are oppositely charged ions. For covalent bonding the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons. For metallic bonding the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons.
Ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.
Covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.
Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.
Students should be able to explain chemical bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and the transfer or sharing of electrons.

los.t: Name the three types of strong chemical bond and the particles involved in each

k.t: There are three types of strong chemical bonds: ionic, covalent and metallic.
For ionic bonding the particles are oppositely charged ions.
For covalent bonding the particles are atoms which share pairs of electrons.
For metallic bonding the particles are atoms which share delocalised electrons.
Strong = forces within a structure; do not confuse with weak intermolecular forces between molecules (4.2.2.4).

los.t: State where ionic bonding occurs

k.t: Ionic bonding occurs in compounds formed from metals combined with non-metals.
NaCl, MgO, CaCl2, K2O.

los.t: State where covalent bonding occurs

k.t: Covalent bonding occurs in most non-metallic elements and in compounds of non-metals.
H2, O2, diamond, graphite (elements); H2O, CO2, CH4, SiO2 (compounds).

los.t: State where metallic bonding occurs

k.t: Metallic bonding occurs in metallic elements and alloys.

los.t: Explain chemical bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and the transfer or sharing of electrons

k.t: Students should be able to explain chemical bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and the transfer or sharing of electrons.

Ionic = transfer of electrons then electrostatic attraction between + and – ions. Covalent = shared pair attracted to both nuclei. Metallic = attraction between positive ions and delocalised electrons.

paras.text: When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred. Metal atoms lose electrons to become positively charged ions. Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negatively charged ions. The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas (Group 0).
notes: Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two- dimensional representations of 3D objects.

paras.text: The electron transfer during the formation of an ionic compound can be represented by a dot and cross diagram, eg for sodium chloride: [Figure in specification — dot and cross diagram: a sodium atom (2,8,1) and a chlorine atom (2,8,7); the outer electron of sodium is transferred to chlorine giving a sodium ion [Na]⁺ (2,8) and a chloride ion [Cl]⁻ (2,8,8) shown in square brackets with charges]
Students should be able to draw dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds formed by metals in Groups 1 and 2 with non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.
The charge on the ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 relates to the group number of the element in the periodic table.
Students should be able to work out the charge on the ions of metals and non-metals from the group number of the element, limited to the metals in Groups 1 and 2, and non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.

los.t: Describe electron transfer between metal and non-metal atoms

k.t: When a metal atom reacts with a non-metal atom electrons in the outer shell of the metal atom are transferred.
Metal atoms lose electrons to become positively charged ions.
Non-metal atoms gain electrons to become negatively charged ions.
OIL RIG (HT): Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain of electrons – metal atoms are oxidised, non-metal atoms reduced.

los.t: State that Group 1, 2, 6 and 7 ions have noble gas electronic structures

k.t: The ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 have the electronic structure of a noble gas (Group 0).
Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects (MS 5b).
Na⁺ 2,8 (like neon); Mg²⁺ 2,8; Cl⁻ 2,8,8 (like argon); O²⁻ 2,8 (like neon).

los.t: Represent electron transfer with a dot and cross diagram for sodium chloride

k.t: The electron transfer during the formation of an ionic compound can be represented by a dot and cross diagram, eg for sodium chloride (figure in specification).
Show outer shells only or all shells; transferred electron changes symbol (dot→cross); ions in square brackets with the charge top right; the new outer shell of the non-metal ion is full.

los.t: Draw dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds of Group 1/2 metals with Group 6/7 non-metals

k.t: Students should be able to draw dot and cross diagrams for ionic compounds formed by metals in Groups 1 and 2 with non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.
NaCl, MgCl2 (one Mg gives one electron to each of two Cl), Na2O (two Na each give one electron to one O), MgO, CaO, K2O, Li2O, CaF2, MgBr2 etc.
For 2:1 compounds draw all three ions with brackets and charges; balance total + and – charge.

los.t: Relate the charge on an ion to the group number (Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7 only)

k.t: The charge on the ions produced by metals in Groups 1 and 2 and by non-metals in Groups 6 and 7 relates to the group number of the element in the periodic table.
Work out the charge on the ions of metals and non-metals from the group number of the element, limited to the metals in Groups 1 and 2, and non-metals in Groups 6 and 7.
Group 1 → 1+; Group 2 → 2+; Group 6 → 2–; Group 7 → 1–.

The specification limits this to Groups 1, 2, 6 and 7. Charges of other ions (e.g. Al³⁺, Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu²⁺, Ag⁺, Zn²⁺, N³⁻) are learned as needed elsewhere (e.g. formulae of compounds) – the group-number rule only guaranteed for the four groups.

paras.text: An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions. Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions. These forces act in all directions in the lattice and this is called ionic bonding.
notes: MS 5b Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects.

paras.text: The structure of sodium chloride can be represented in the following forms: [Figure in specification — (a) ball and stick model of the sodium chloride lattice and (b) space-filling model, with key showing Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions] Students should be able to: • deduce that a compound is ionic from a diagram of its structure in one of the specified forms • describe the limitations of using dot and cross, ball and stick, two and three-dimensional diagrams to represent a giant ionic structure • work out the empirical formula of an ionic compound from a given model or diagram that shows the ions in the structure.
Students should be familiar with the structure of sodium chloride but do not need to know the structures of other ionic compounds.

los.t: Describe an ionic compound as a giant structure of ions

k.t: An ionic compound is a giant structure of ions.
Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects (MS 5b).

los.t: Explain ionic bonding as strong electrostatic forces acting in all directions in the lattice

k.t: Ionic compounds are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.
These forces act in all directions in the lattice and this is called ionic bonding.
Lattice = regular, repeating 3D arrangement of ions.

los.t: Represent the structure of sodium chloride in the specified forms

k.t: The structure of sodium chloride can be represented in the following forms: ball and stick and space-filling models (figure in specification).
Alternate Na⁺ and Cl⁻ in a cubic lattice; each ion surrounded by oppositely charged ions.

los.t: Deduce that a compound is ionic from a diagram of its structure

k.t: Deduce that a compound is ionic from a diagram of its structure in one of the specified forms.
Look for a regular lattice with two types of particle alternating in all directions and a key showing charges.

los.t: Describe the limitations of dot and cross, ball and stick and 2D/3D diagrams for giant ionic structures

k.t: Describe the limitations of using dot and cross, ball and stick, two and three-dimensional diagrams to represent a giant ionic structure.

Dot and cross – shows only electron transfer between a few ions, not the giant structure. Ball and stick – shows ions as small balls with gaps, bonds as sticks that do not exist (forces act in all directions), gives wrong impression of ion size and spacing. 2D diagrams – cannot show the 3D arrangement. Space-filling – hides the internal arrangement and does not show the forces.

los.t: Work out the empirical formula of an ionic compound from a model or diagram

k.t: Work out the empirical formula of an ionic compound from a given model or diagram that shows the ions in the structure (MS 1a, 1c).
Count each type of ion in the model (or use the repeating unit) → simplest whole-number ratio. Check charges balance.
1 Mg²⁺ to 2 Cl⁻ gives MgCl2. 2 Na⁺ to 1 O²⁻ gives Na2O. Be careful to count ions shared between unit cells only if the diagram shows them.

los.t: Know that only the structure of sodium chloride is required

k.t: Students should be familiar with the structure of sodium chloride but do not need to know the structures of other ionic compounds.

paras.text: When atoms share pairs of electrons, they form covalent bonds. These bonds between atoms are strong.
notes: Recognise substances as small molecules, polymers or giant structures from diagrams showing their bonding.

paras.text: Covalently bonded substances may consist of small molecules.
Students should be able to recognise common substances that consist of small molecules from their chemical formula.
Some covalently bonded substances have very large molecules, such as polymers.
Some covalently bonded substances have giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide.

The covalent bonds in molecules and giant structures can be represented in the following forms: [Figure in specification — ammonia, NH₃, shown as a dot and cross diagram, as a displayed formula (N bonded to three H by single lines) and as a 3D ball-and-stick model] Polymers can be represented in the form: [Figure in specification — poly(ethene) repeat unit in brackets with subscript n] where n is a large number.

k.t: When atoms share pairs of electrons, they form covalent bonds.
These bonds between atoms are strong.

los.t: State that covalently bonded substances may consist of small molecules

k.t: Covalently bonded substances may consist of small molecules.

los.t: Recognise common small-molecule substances from their chemical formula

k.t: Students should be able to recognise common substances that consist of small molecules from their chemical formula.
H2, O2, N2, Cl2, H2O, CO2, NH3, CH4, HCl, C2H6, ethanol C2H5OH (formulae with only non-metal symbols and small numbers of atoms).
Metal + non-metal formula = ionic, not small molecule. Very large or repeating formulae = polymer or giant covalent.

los.t: Describe polymers as very large covalent molecules

k.t: Some covalently bonded substances have very large molecules, such as polymers.

los.t: Describe giant covalent structures

k.t: Some covalently bonded substances have giant covalent structures, such as diamond and silicon dioxide.

los.t: Represent covalent bonds in the specified forms, including polymers as a repeating unit

k.t: The covalent bonds in molecules and giant structures can be represented in the following forms: dot and cross, displayed formula and 3D model (ammonia shown in figure).
Polymers can be represented in the form: repeat unit in brackets with subscript n, where n is a large number.
Poly(ethene): ( –CH2–CH2– )n. The bonds at each end of the brackets continue.

los.t: Draw dot and cross diagrams for H2, Cl2, O2, N2, HCl, H2O, NH3 and CH4

k.t: Draw dot and cross diagrams for the molecules of hydrogen, chlorine, oxygen, nitrogen, hydrogen chloride, water, ammonia and methane.

H2 – one shared pair. Cl2 – one shared pair; each Cl keeps 3 lone pairs. O2 – double bond (two shared pairs). N2 – triple bond (three shared pairs), each N keeps one lone pair. HCl – one shared pair, Cl has 3 lone pairs. H2O – O with two bonds and two lone pairs. NH3 – N with three bonds and one lone pair. CH4 – C with four single bonds, no lone pairs.
Show only outer shells; every atom (except H) ends with 8 outer electrons; H ends with 2.

los.t: Represent covalent bonds using a line for each single bond in molecules, polymer repeat units and giant covalent structures

k.t: Represent the covalent bonds in small molecules, in the repeating units of polymers and in part of giant covalent structures, using a line to represent a single bond.
Displayed formula: H–Cl, H–O–H, H–N(–H)–H; each line = one shared pair; double bond drawn as two lines (O=O, O=C=O) as seen in later topics.

los.t: Describe the limitations of dot and cross, ball and stick and 2D/3D diagrams for molecules or giant structures

k.t: Describe the limitations of using dot and cross, ball and stick, two and three-dimensional diagrams to represent molecules or giant structures.

Dot and cross – does not show shape or relative sizes. Displayed 2D formula – does not show the true 3D shape or bond angles. Ball and stick – bonds drawn as sticks with length that does not match reality; atoms look separated. 3D models/giant structures – can show only a small part of a structure that continues.

los.t: Deduce the molecular formula of a substance from a model or diagram

k.t: Deduce the molecular formula of a substance from a given model or diagram in these forms showing the atoms and bonds in the molecule.
Count the atoms of each element in the diagram → write symbols with subscripts (e.g. 2 C + 6 H → C2H6). For a polymer use the repeating unit.
MS 5b.

paras.text: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.
notes: Recognise substances as metallic giant structures from diagrams showing their bonding.

paras.text: The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure. The sharing of delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds. The bonding in metals may be represented in the following form: [Figure in specification — regular lattice of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons]
notes: Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two- dimensional representations of 3D objects.

los.t: Describe metals as giant structures of atoms in a regular pattern

k.t: Metals consist of giant structures of atoms arranged in a regular pattern.
WS 1.2. Recognise substances as metallic giant structures from diagrams showing their bonding.

los.t: Explain metallic bonding in terms of delocalised electrons

k.t: The electrons in the outer shell of metal atoms are delocalised and so are free to move through the whole structure.
The sharing of delocalised electrons gives rise to strong metallic bonds.
Positive metal ions held in a lattice by electrostatic attraction to the 'sea' of delocalised electrons.

los.t: Represent metallic bonding in the specified form

k.t: The bonding in metals may be represented in the following form: regular lattice of positive ions in a sea of delocalised electrons (figure in specification).

Draw rows of circles marked + with small – dots/e⁻ between them.

sections.title: How bonding and structure are related to the properties of substances

paras.text: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas. Melting and freezing take place at the melting point, boiling and condensing take place at the boiling point.
notes: MS 5b Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects.

paras.text: The three states of matter can be represented by a simple model. In this model, particles are represented by small solid spheres. Particle theory can help to explain melting, boiling, freezing and condensing. [Figure in specification — particle diagrams of a solid (particles touching in a regular arrangement), a liquid (particles touching, irregular arrangement) and a gas (particles far apart, random)]

The amount of energy needed to change state from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas depends on the strength of the forces between the particles of the substance. The nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance. The stronger the forces between the particles the higher the melting point and boiling point of the substance.
(HT only) Limitations of the simple model above include that in the model there are no forces, that all particles are represented as spheres and that the spheres are solid.

Students should be able to: • predict the states of substances at different temperatures given appropriate data • explain the different temperatures at which changes of state occur in terms of energy transfers and types of bonding • recognise that atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of materials • (HT only) explain the limitations of the particle theory in relation to changes of state when particles are represented by solid inelastic spheres which have no forces between them.

los.t: Name the three states of matter and the processes between them

k.t: The three states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
Melting and freezing take place at the melting point, boiling and condensing take place at the boiling point.
Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects (MS 5b).
Solid → liquid melting; liquid → solid freezing; liquid → gas boiling (evaporating); gas → liquid condensing. Melting point = freezing point for a pure substance.

los.t: Represent the three states of matter using the simple particle model

k.t: The three states of matter can be represented by a simple model. In this model, particles are represented by small solid spheres.
Particle theory can help to explain melting, boiling, freezing and condensing.

Solid – particles close together, regular pattern, vibrate about fixed positions. Liquid – close together, irregular arrangement, can move/slide past each other. Gas – far apart, random arrangement, move quickly in all directions.

los.t: Relate energy needed for state changes to the strength of forces between particles

k.t: The amount of energy needed to change state from solid to liquid and from liquid to gas depends on the strength of the forces between the particles of the substance.
The nature of the particles involved depends on the type of bonding and the structure of the substance.
The stronger the forces between the particles the higher the melting point and boiling point of the substance.
During a change of state the energy transferred breaks/overcomes forces between particles; temperature stays constant at the change of state.

los.t: State the limitations of the simple particle model

k.t: (HT only) Limitations of the simple model above include that in the model there are no forces, that all particles are represented as spheres and that the spheres are solid.

los.t: Predict states of substances at different temperatures from data

k.t: Predict the states of substances at different temperatures given appropriate data.
Compare the temperature with the melting and boiling points: below mp = solid; between mp and bp = liquid; above bp = gas.

los.t: Explain different change-of-state temperatures in terms of energy transfers and bonding

k.t: Explain the different temperatures at which changes of state occur in terms of energy transfers and types of bonding.
Ionic/giant covalent/metallic – many strong bonds to break → high mp/bp. Simple molecular – only weak intermolecular forces overcome → low mp/bp (the covalent bonds are not broken).

los.t: Recognise that atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of materials

k.t: Recognise that atoms themselves do not have the bulk properties of materials.
A single copper atom is not itself shiny, hard or a conductor: bulk properties come from the structure/bonding of many atoms. Atoms do not melt or become 'hot' individually.

los.t: Explain the limitations of particle theory for changes of state

k.t: (HT only) Explain the limitations of the particle theory in relation to changes of state when particles are represented by solid inelastic spheres which have no forces between them.

With no forces in the model it cannot explain why different substances have different melting/boiling points, why energy is needed to melt/boil, or why particles stay together in solids/liquids. Particles are not solid spheres, they have structure (e.g. molecules, ions) and have different sizes/shapes.

paras.text: In chemical equations, the three states of matter are shown as (s), (l) and (g), with (aq) for aqueous solutions.
Students should be able to include appropriate state symbols in chemical equations for the reactions in this specification.

los.t: State the symbols for the states of matter

k.t: In chemical equations, the three states of matter are shown as (s), (l) and (g), with (aq) for aqueous solutions.
(aq) = dissolved in water.

los.t: Include appropriate state symbols in equations for reactions in the specification

Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl2(aq) + H2(g). CaCO3(s) → CaO(s) + CO2(g). Water as a product of a reaction at room temperature is (l); steam = (g).

paras.text: Ionic compounds have regular structures (giant ionic lattices) in which there are strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.
These compounds have high melting points and high boiling points because of the large amounts of energy needed to break the many strong bonds.
When melted or dissolved in water, ionic compounds conduct electricity because the ions are free to move and so charge can flow.
Knowledge of the structures of specific ionic compounds other than sodium chloride is not required.

los.t: Describe the structure of ionic compounds as giant ionic lattices

k.t: Ionic compounds have regular structures (giant ionic lattices) in which there are strong electrostatic forces of attraction in all directions between oppositely charged ions.

los.t: Explain high melting and boiling points of ionic compounds

k.t: These compounds have high melting points and high boiling points because of the large amounts of energy needed to break the many strong bonds.

los.t: Explain electrical conductivity of ionic compounds when melted or dissolved

k.t: When melted or dissolved in water, ionic compounds conduct electricity because the ions are free to move and so charge can flow.

los.t: Know that structures of ionic compounds other than sodium chloride are not required

k.t: Knowledge of the structures of specific ionic compounds other than sodium chloride is not required.

paras.text: Substances that consist of small molecules are usually gases or liquids that have relatively low melting points and boiling points.
These substances have only weak forces between the molecules (intermolecular forces). It is these intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds, when the substance melts or boils.
The intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
These substances do not conduct electricity because the molecules do not have an overall electric charge.
Students should be able to use the idea that intermolecular forces are weak compared with covalent bonds to explain the bulk properties of molecular substances.

los.t: State typical physical state and melting/boiling points of small-molecule substances

k.t: Substances that consist of small molecules are usually gases or liquids that have relatively low melting points and boiling points.

los.t: Explain that intermolecular forces (not covalent bonds) are overcome on melting/boiling

k.t: These substances have only weak forces between the molecules (intermolecular forces).
It is these intermolecular forces that are overcome, not the covalent bonds, when the substance melts or boils.

los.t: Relate melting and boiling points to molecular size

k.t: The intermolecular forces increase with the size of the molecules, so larger molecules have higher melting and boiling points.
Links to Group 7 (Cl2 gas, Br2 liquid, I2 solid) and alkanes (longer chain → higher boiling point).

los.t: Explain why small-molecule substances do not conduct electricity

k.t: These substances do not conduct electricity because the molecules do not have an overall electric charge.

paras.text: Chemists use quantitative analysis to determine the formulae of compounds and the equations for reactions. Given this information, analysts can then use quantitative methods to determine the purity of chemical samples and to monitor the yield from chemical reactions.

Chemical equations provide a means of representing chemical reactions and are a key way for chemists to communicate chemical ideas.

paras.text: The percentage atom economy of a reaction is calculated using the balanced equation for the reaction as follows: Atom economy = (Relative formula mass of desired product from equation ÷ Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) × 100. Students should be able to: • calculate the atom economy of a reaction to form a desired product from the balanced equation • (HT only) explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to produce a specified product given appropriate data such as atom economy (if not calculated), yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products.
notes: Change the subject of an equation.

paras.text: Understanding of chemical changes began when people began experimenting with chemical reactions in a systematic way and organizing their results logically. Knowing about these different chemical changes meant that scientists could begin to predict exactly what new substances would be formed and use this knowledge to develop a wide range of different materials and processes. It also helped biochemists to understand the complex reactions that take place in living organisms. The extraction of important resources from the earth makes use of the way that some elements and compounds react with each other and how easily they can be ‘pulled apart’.
Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides. The reactions are oxidation reactions because the metals gain oxygen.
Students should be able to explain reduction and oxidation in terms of loss or gain of oxygen.

los.t: Describe the reaction of metals with oxygen to form metal oxides

k.t: Metals react with oxygen to produce metal oxides.
2Mg + O2 → 2MgO; 4Al + 3O2 → 2Al2O3; 2Cu + O2 → 2CuO. Observations: magnesium burns with a bright white flame leaving white magnesium oxide.

k.t: The reactions are oxidation reactions because the metals gain oxygen.

los.t: Explain reduction and oxidation in terms of loss or gain of oxygen

paras.text: When metals react with other substances the metal atoms form positive ions. The reactivity of a metal is related to its tendency to form positive ions. Metals can be arranged in order of their reactivity in a reactivity series. The metals potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, zinc, iron and copper can be put in order of their reactivity from their reactions with water and dilute acids.

A more reactive metal can displace a less reactive metal from a compound.

The reactions of metals with water and acids are limited to room temperature and do not include reactions with steam.

los.t: Recall and describe the reactions, if any, of the eight metals with water or dilute acids and order them

With cold water: K – violent, lilac flame, hydrogen ignites; Na – vigorous fizzing, melts into a ball; Li – steady fizzing; Ca – steady fizzing, solution turns cloudy (calcium hydroxide). Mg, Zn, Fe, Cu – no visible reaction with cold water (specification limits to room temperature, no steam).
With dilute hydrochloric/sulfuric acid: Mg – rapid fizzing; Zn – steady fizzing; Fe – slow fizzing; Cu – no reaction; Li, Na, K, Ca – react violently/explosively (not usually done).
metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen (2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2; Ca + 2H2O → Ca(OH)2 + H2). metal + acid → salt + hydrogen (Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2).

sections.title: Neutralisation of acids and salt production

paras.text: Acids are neutralised by alkalis (eg soluble metal hydroxides) and bases (eg insoluble metal hydroxides and metal oxides) to produce salts and water, and by metal carbonates to produce salts, water and carbon dioxide.

The particular salt produced in any reaction between an acid and a base or alkali depends on: • the acid used (hydrochloric acid produces chlorides, nitric acid produces nitrates, sulfuric acid produces sulfates) • the positive ions in the base, alkali or carbonate.

Acids are neutralised by metal carbonates to produce salts, water and carbon dioxide.
acid + alkali/base → salt + water; acid + metal carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O; H2SO4 + CuO → CuSO4 + H2O; 2HCl + CaCO3 → CaCl2 + H2O + CO2.

paras.text: When an ionic compound is melted or dissolved in water, the ions are free to move about within the liquid or solution. These liquids and solutions are able to conduct electricity and are called electrolytes.

Passing an electric current through electrolytes causes the ions to move to the electrodes. Positively charged ions move to the negative electrode (the cathode), and negatively charged ions move to the positive electrode (the anode). Ions are discharged at the electrodes producing elements. This process is called electrolysis.

(HT only) Throughout Section 4.4.3 Higher Tier students should be able to write half equations for the reactions occurring at the electrodes during electrolysis, and may be required to complete and balance supplied half equations.

paras.text: Energy changes are an important part of chemical reactions. The interaction of particles often involves transfers of energy due to the breaking and formation of bonds. Reactions in which energy is released to the surroundings are exothermic reactions, while those that take in thermal energy are endothermic. These interactions between particles can produce heating or cooling effects that are used in a range of everyday applications. Some interactions between ions in an electrolyte result in the production of electricity. Cells and batteries use these chemical reactions to provide electricity. Electricity can also be used to decompose ionic substances and is a useful means of producing elements that are too expensive to extract any other way.

sections.title: The rate and extent of chemical change

paras.text: Chemical reactions can occur at vastly different rates. Whilst the reactivity of chemicals is a significant factor in how fast chemical reactions proceed, there are many variables that can be manipulated in order to speed them up or slow them down. Chemical reactions may also be reversible and therefore the effect of different variables needs to be established in order to identify how to maximise the yield of desired product. Understanding energy changes that accompany chemical reactions is important for this process. In industry, chemists and chemical engineers determine the effect of different variables on reaction rate and yield of product. Whilst there may be compromises to be made, they carry out optimisation processes to ensure that enough product is produced within a sufficient time, and in an energy-efficient way.

The rate of a chemical reaction can be found by measuring the quantity of a reactant used or the quantity of product formed over time: mean rate of reaction = quantity of reactant used ÷ time taken; mean rate of reaction = quantity of product formed ÷ time taken.

paras.text: Collision theory explains how various factors affect rates of reactions. Increasing the temperature increases the frequency of collisions and makes the collisions more energetic, and so increases the rate of reaction.

paras.text: The chemistry of carbon compounds is so important that it forms a separate branch of chemistry. A great variety of carbon compounds is possible because carbon atoms can form chains and rings linked by C-C bonds. This branch of chemistry gets its name from the fact that the main sources of organic compounds are living, or once-living materials from plants and animals. These sources include fossil fuels which are a major source of feedstock for the petrochemical industry. Chemists are able to take organic molecules and modify them in many ways to make new and useful materials such as polymers, pharmaceuticals, perfumes and flavourings, dyes and detergents.

paras.text: Analysts have developed a range of qualitative tests to detect specific chemicals. The tests are based on reactions that produce a gas with distinctive properties, or a colour change or an insoluble solid that appears as a precipitate.

Instrumental methods provide fast, sensitive and accurate means of analysing chemicals, and are particularly useful when the amount of chemical being analysed is small. Forensic scientists and drug control scientists rely on such instrumental methods in their work.
In chemistry, a pure substance is a single element or compound, not mixed with any other substance.
Pure elements and compounds melt and boil at specific temperatures. Melting point and boiling point data can be used to distinguish pure substances from mixtures.
In everyday language, a pure substance can mean a substance that has had nothing added to it, so it is unadulterated and in its natural state, eg pure milk.
Students should be able to use melting point and boiling point data to distinguish pure from impure substances.

sections.title: The composition and evolution of the Earth's atmosphere
The proportions of different gases in the atmosphere

paras.text: For 200 million years, the proportions of different gases in the atmosphere have been much the same as they are today: • about four-fifths (approximately 80%) nitrogen • about one-fifth (approximately 20%) oxygen • small proportions of various other gases, including carbon dioxide, water vapour and noble gases.

paras.text: Theories about what was in the Earth’s early atmosphere and how the atmosphere was formed have changed and developed over time. Evidence for the early atmosphere is limited because of the time scale of 4.6 billion years.

One theory suggests that during the first billion years of the Earth’s existence there was intense volcanic activity that released gases that formed the early atmosphere and water vapour that condensed to form the oceans. At the start of this period the Earth’s atmosphere may have been like the atmospheres of Mars and Venus today, consisting of mainly carbon dioxide with little or no oxygen gas.
Volcanoes also produced nitrogen which gradually built up in the atmosphere and there may have been small proportions of methane and ammonia.

When the oceans formed carbon dioxide dissolved in the water and carbonates were precipitated producing sediments, reducing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. No knowledge of other theories is required.
Students should be able to, given appropriate information, interpret evidence and evaluate different theories about the Earth’s early atmosphere.

paras.text: Industries use the Earth’s natural resources to manufacture useful products. Pollution, disposal of waste products and changing land use has a significant effect on the environment, and environmental chemists study how human activity has affected the Earth’s natural cycles, and how damaging effects can be minimised.

paras.text: Water of appropriate quality is essential for life. For humans, drinking water should have sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes. Water that is safe to drink is called potable water. Potable water is not pure water in the chemical sense because it contains dissolved substances.
The methods used to produce potable water depend on available supplies of water and local conditions.

In the United Kingdom (UK), rain provides water with low levels of dissolved substances (fresh water) that collects in the ground and in lakes and rivers, and most potable water is produced by: • choosing an appropriate source of fresh water • passing the water through filter beds • sterilising.
Sterilising agents used for potable water include chlorine, ozone or ultraviolet light.

If supplies of fresh water are limited, desalination of salty water or sea water may be required. Desalination can be done by distillation or by processes that use membranes such as reverse osmosis. These processes require large amounts of energy.

Students should be able to: • distinguish between potable water and pure water • describe the differences in treatment of ground water and salty water • give reasons for the steps used to produce potable water.

sections.title: Alternative methods of extracting metals (HT only)

paras.text: The Earth’s resources of metal ores are limited.

Copper ores are becoming scarce and new ways of extracting copper from low-grade ores include phytomining, and bioleaching. These methods avoid traditional mining methods of digging, moving and disposing of large amounts of rock.
Phytomining uses plants to absorb metal compounds. The plants are harvested and then burned to produce ash that contains metal compounds.
Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce leachate solutions that contain metal compounds.
The metal compounds can be processed to obtain the metal. For example, copper can be obtained from solutions of copper compounds by displacement using scrap iron or by electrolysis.

sections.title: Ways of reducing the use of resources

paras.text: The reduction in use, reuse and recycling of materials by end users reduces the use of limited resources, use of energy sources, waste and environmental impacts.

Metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics are produced from limited raw materials. Much of the energy for the processes comes from limited resources. Obtaining raw materials from the Earth by quarrying and mining causes environmental impacts.
Some products, such as glass bottles, can be reused. Glass bottles can be crushed and melted to make different glass products. Other products cannot be reused and so are recycled for a different use.

Metals can be recycled by melting and recasting or reforming into different products. The amount of separation required for recycling depends on the material and the properties required of the final product. For example, some scrap steel can be added to iron from a blast furnace to reduce the amount of iron that needs to be extracted from iron ore.

paras.text: The raw materials for the Haber process are nitrogen and hydrogen.
Students should be able to recall a source for the nitrogen and a source for the hydrogen used in the Haber process.

sections.title: Production and uses of NPK fertilisers

paras.text: Compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are used as fertilisers to improve agricultural productivity. NPK fertilisers contain compounds of all three elements.

Industrial production of NPK fertilisers can be achieved using a variety of raw materials in several integrated processes. NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of the elements.
Ammonia can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are obtained by mining, but phosphate rock cannot be used directly as a fertiliser.
Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid or sulfuric acid to produce soluble salts that can be used as fertilisers.

Students should be able to: • recall the names of the salts produced when phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid, sulfuric acid and phosphoric acid • compare the industrial production of fertilisers with laboratory preparations of the same compounds, given appropriate information.

paras.text: The complex and diverse phenomena of the natural world can be described in terms of a small number of key ideas in chemistry.

These key ideas are of universal application, and we have embedded them throughout the subject content. They underpin many aspects of the science assessment and will therefore be assessed across all papers.

These ideas include: • matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atoms called elements • elements show periodic relationships in their chemical and physical properties • these periodic properties can be explained in terms of the atomic structure of the elements • atoms bond by either transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing electrons • the shapes of molecules (groups of atoms bonded together) and the way giant structures are arranged is of great importance in terms of the way they behave
• there are barriers to reaction so reactions occur at different rates • chemical reactions take place in only three different ways: • proton transfer • electron transfer • electron sharing
• energy is conserved in chemical reactions so can therefore be neither created or destroyed.
