PURPOSE: To prepare a pure, dry sample of a soluble salt (copper(II) sulfate crystals) by reacting an insoluble base (copper(II) oxide) or carbonate with a dilute acid (sulfuric acid), using a Bunsen burner to heat the acid and a water bath or electric heater to evaporate the solution.
APPARATUS: Dilute sulfuric acid (about 1 mol/dm³), copper(II) oxide (or copper(II) carbonate), spatula
100 cm³ beaker, measuring cylinder (25 cm³), glass stirring rod
Bunsen burner, tripod, gauze, heatproof mat; or electric heater / hot plate
Water bath (beaker of water) or electric water bath
Filter funnel, filter paper, conical flask or second beaker
Evaporating basin, glass rod, crystallising dish, tongs
Distilled water, filter paper or paper towels for drying
Eye protection
METHOD: Measure about 25 cm³ of dilute sulfuric acid into a beaker and warm it gently with a Bunsen burner (do not boil).

Add a spatula of copper(II) oxide, stir and wait until it has stopped dissolving. Repeat adding small amounts until some solid remains at the bottom (the base is in excess, so all the acid has been used up). A blue solution forms.
Allow the mixture to cool slightly, then filter it to remove the excess copper(II) oxide. The blue solution that passes through is the filtrate (copper(II) sulfate solution).

Pour the filtrate into an evaporating basin and heat it gently over a beaker of boiling water (water bath) or on an electric heater until about half of the water has evaporated, or until crystals start to form when a drop is placed on a cold glass rod.
Stop heating and leave the basin to cool and crystallise slowly (leave overnight for larger crystals).
Remove the crystals by filtering, wash with a very small amount of cold distilled water and dry them between sheets of filter paper (or in a warm oven).
IV: None – this is a preparation rather than a fair-test investigation (the quantity of acid and base can be changed to compare yields).
DV: The mass and appearance of the crystals made (yield and purity).
CV: Volume and concentration of acid
Temperature when reacting (warm, not boiling)
Method of evaporation (water bath, not direct heating to dryness)
Cooling rate when crystallising
SAFETY: Wear eye protection throughout; dilute sulfuric acid is an irritant.
Copper(II) oxide and copper(II) sulfate are harmful and dangerous to the environment – avoid contact with skin and do not pour solutions down the sink.
Do not boil the acid – it can spit; use tongs for hot containers.
Do not heat the evaporating basin to dryness (spitting and decomposition of the salt); use a water bath.
RESULTS: The black copper(II) oxide dissolves in the warm acid to give a blue solution of copper(II) sulfate; the excess black solid stays on the filter paper.
Blue crystals of hydrated copper(II) sulfate (CuSO4·5H2O) form on cooling.
A copper(II) carbonate version fizzes as carbon dioxide is released (green solid dissolves).
ANALYSIS: Equation (base): CuO + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O. Equation (carbonate): CuCO3 + H2SO4 → CuSO4 + H2O + CO2.
Ionic equation (HT): CuO + 2H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + H2O.
Percentage yield (chemistry only) = actual mass of crystals ÷ theoretical mass × 100, using moles of the limiting reactant (the acid) from 4.3.
ERRORS: Not all the solid is converted or recovered, so the yield is lower: some solution stays on the filter paper and the glassware.
Crystals contain water or are damp if not dried properly, so the mass is too high; heating to dryness can remove water of crystallisation.
If the acid is not fully used up (insufficient solid added) the product is contaminated with acid.
Improvements: use excess solid and make sure the last portion no longer reacts; wash residue; cool slowly for larger, purer crystals.
EXAM: Why is the insoluble solid added in excess? (All the acid is used up; the excess can be removed by filtering.)
Why filter? (To remove excess insoluble solid.) Why use a water bath? (Even, gentle heating; prevents spitting/decomposition.)
Why leave the solution to crystallise rather than evaporating to dryness? (Larger, purer crystals; the salt may decompose or lose water of crystallisation.)
How could you tell the reaction had finished? (Solid stops disappearing/fizzing stops.)
Describe how to make a different named salt (e.g. zinc sulfate from zinc oxide, magnesium chloride from magnesium oxide).
Link: 4.4.2.3 Soluble salts; AT 2, 3, 4, 6.

PURPOSE: (Chemistry only) To determine the reacting volumes of solutions of a strong acid and a strong alkali by titration and, at Higher Tier, to calculate the concentration of one solution in mol/dm³ and g/dm³ from the reacting volumes and the known concentration of the other.
APPARATUS: Burette (50 cm³) and stand with white tile underneath, burette clamp
25.0 cm³ pipette and pipette filler
250 cm³ conical flasks (several)
Small funnel for filling the burette
Hydrochloric acid of known concentration (e.g. 0.100 mol/dm³) and sodium hydroxide solution of unknown concentration (or vice versa)
Indicator: methyl orange or phenolphthalein; dropping pipette
Distilled water wash bottle, eye protection
METHOD: Rinse the burette with the acid and the pipette with the alkali, then rinse the conical flask with distilled water only.
Fill the burette with acid (use a funnel, then remove it) to above the 0.00 mark and run some through the tap to fill the jet – no air bubbles. Record the initial reading to 0.05 cm³.
Use the pipette and filler to transfer exactly 25.0 cm³ of the alkali into a conical flask. Add a few drops of indicator and place on a white tile.
Add the acid from the burette quickly at first, swirling continuously, until the indicator is close to changing colour (rough titration). Record the final reading.
Repeat accurately: add acid drop by drop near the end-point until one drop gives a permanent colour change; record the final reading and calculate the titre (final – initial).
Repeat until you have at least two concordant results (titres within 0.10 cm³ of each other). Calculate the mean of the concordant titres (ignore the rough/anomalous titre).
IV: The volume of acid added (the end-point is the volume of acid at which the colour changes).
DV: The volume of acid needed to neutralise exactly 25.0 cm³ of alkali (titre); the colour of the indicator.
CV: Volume of alkali in the flask (25.0 cm³ by pipette)
Concentration of acid and of alkali
Same indicator and the same number of drops
Swirling and reading the burette at eye level to the bottom of the meniscus
SAFETY: Wear eye protection; acids and alkalis at these concentrations are irritant (sodium hydroxide can be corrosive).
Use a pipette filler – never suck solutions by mouth.
Mop up spills straight away; wash hands after use.
RESULTS: Methyl orange: yellow in alkali, orange at the end-point, red in acid. Phenolphthalein: pink in alkali, colourless in acid.
Concordant titres are within 0.10 cm³ (e.g. 22.40, 22.45 cm³).
Typical outcome for equal concentrations: roughly equal volumes of acid and alkali are needed (1:1 reaction).
ANALYSIS: Mean titre = (sum of concordant titres) ÷ number of titres.

HT: Example: 25.0 cm³ of NaOH (unknown) is neutralised by 22.50 cm³ of 0.100 mol/dm³ HCl. n(HCl) = 0.100 × 0.02250 = 0.002250 mol. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O (1:1) so n(NaOH) = 0.002250 mol in 0.0250 dm³; c(NaOH) = 0.002250 ÷ 0.0250 = 0.0900 mol/dm³.
Convert to g/dm³: multiply by Mr (NaOH 40): 0.0900 × 40 = 3.60 g/dm³.
Use the balancing numbers if the ratio is not 1:1 (e.g. H2SO4 + 2NaOH → Na2SO4 + 2H2O).
Give answers to an appropriate number of significant figures (usually 3).
ERRORS: Overshooting the end-point (adding acid too quickly near the end) – add dropwise and use a white tile.
Parallax when reading the burette – read at eye level, bottom of meniscus.
Air bubble in the burette jet/stem – fill the jet before the first reading.
Not rinsing equipment with the right solutions – dilutes or contaminates solutions.
Pipette not filled exactly to the line; leaving the funnel in the burette (drips).
Improvements: repeat until concordant, use a burette with smaller graduations, add a few drops only of indicator, use a pH meter to detect the end-point.
EXAM: Describe the method for a titration, including why a pipette and a white tile are used.
Why is the first (rough) titration not included in the mean? (Overshoots/imprecise.)
Why use an indicator that has a sharp colour change rather than universal indicator?
Calculate unknown concentration (mol/dm³ and g/dm³) – HT only.
State what 'concordant' means and why more than one titration is carried out.
Link: 4.4.2.5 and 4.3.4; AT 1 and 8.

PURPOSE: To investigate what happens when aqueous solutions are electrolysed using inert electrodes, developing and testing a hypothesis about which products form at each electrode.
APPARATUS: Low-voltage DC power supply (about 4–6 V), leads and crocodile clips
Two inert (graphite/carbon) electrodes
Electrolysis cell: 100 cm³ beaker, or a Petri dish or U-tube with two test tubes to collect gas
Aqueous solutions (about 0.5–1 mol/dm³): copper(II) chloride, sodium chloride, copper(II) sulfate, sodium sulfate (others may be used)
Damp blue litmus paper, wooden splints, test tubes
Eye protection; ventilated area or fume cupboard
METHOD: Pour about 50 cm³ of the first solution into the beaker (or set up the U-tube).
Place the two graphite electrodes so they do not touch, connect them to the power pack and switch on. Record observations at each electrode (bubbles, colour of deposits, smell).

Collect any gas by placing an inverted test tube over each electrode (filled with the solution) for a few minutes. Test: hydrogen – lighted splint pops; oxygen – glowing splint relights; chlorine – damp litmus paper bleached.
Switch off, remove the electrodes and note any deposit. Rinse electrodes before the next solution.
Repeat for each solution and record the products formed at the cathode and anode in a table.
IV: The aqueous solution (the ionic compound dissolved) being electrolysed.
DV: The products formed at the cathode and at the anode (identified by observations and gas tests).
CV: Same electrode material (inert graphite)
Same voltage/current and time
Same concentration and volume of solution
Same distance between the electrodes
SAFETY: Wear eye protection throughout; solutions containing copper are harmful.
Chlorine is toxic and an irritant (especially to asthmatics): use dilute solutions, small volumes, short times and good ventilation or a fume cupboard.
Keep the voltage low (≤ 6 V); do not touch the electrodes while switched on.
Hydrogen is flammable – test small samples away from naked flames.
RESULTS: CuCl2(aq): brown/pink solid copper at the cathode; chlorine at the anode (pungent smell, bleaches damp litmus).
NaCl(aq): hydrogen at the cathode (squeaky pop); chlorine at the anode.
CuSO4(aq): copper at the cathode; oxygen at the anode (relights a glowing splint).
Na2SO4(aq) or dilute H2SO4: hydrogen at the cathode and oxygen at the anode (about 2:1 by volume).
ANALYSIS: Cathode (negative): the metal is produced if it is less reactive than hydrogen; otherwise hydrogen is produced from water.
Anode (positive): halogen is produced if a halide is present; otherwise oxygen from hydroxide ions in water.
HT: half equations, e.g. Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H2; 2Cl⁻ → Cl2 + 2e⁻; 4OH⁻ → O2 + 2H2O + 4e⁻.
Compare results with the hypothesis (e.g. 'the product at the cathode depends on the reactivity of the metal relative to hydrogen') and decide whether it is supported.
ERRORS: Gas products collected at the same time can be mixed or lost; some chlorine dissolves in water, so less gas than expected.
Impurities on electrodes or reaction of electrodes can alter the products.
Observations are qualitative and subjective – improve by using clear gas tests and repeat.
Improvement: use sealed gas collection with syringes/Hoffman voltameter to compare volumes.
EXAM: Predict the products at each electrode for a given aqueous solution and explain why.
Describe the tests for hydrogen, oxygen and chlorine.
Explain why inert electrodes are used.
Develop a hypothesis, write a plan and evaluate results.

PURPOSE: To investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions, e.g. acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations, displacement of metals.
APPARATUS: Polystyrene cup (or two nested cups) with lid, 250 cm³ beaker as stand
Thermometer (0.1 °C resolution, or temperature probe/data logger)
Measuring cylinder (25 or 50 cm³) or burette; balance

Reactants: dilute hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution (neutralisation); metals (magnesium, zinc, iron) with copper(II) sulfate solution (displacement); metal carbonates or hydrogencarbonates with acid; citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate (endothermic)
Stopwatch, spatula, stirring rod, eye protection
METHOD: Place the polystyrene cup in a beaker for support; measure a fixed volume (e.g. 25 cm³) of the first solution into the cup and record its temperature for a few minutes to get a steady starting temperature.
Add a measured volume or mass of the second reactant (e.g. alkali, metal powder), put on the lid, stir with the thermometer and record the temperature every 30 s until it peaks (or falls).
Record the highest (exothermic) or lowest (endothermic) temperature reached and calculate the temperature change.
Repeat for different variables (e.g. type of metal; concentration of acid; volume of alkali added in 5 cm³ steps) and repeat each experiment to find a mean.
IV: The variable being changed (e.g. the type of metal, concentration of the solution, or volume of alkali added).
DV: The maximum (or minimum) temperature change in °C.
CV: Volume and starting temperature of the solution
Mass (or amount) of solid added; surface area of solid (use powders of the same particle size)
Same insulation, lid and stirring
Same concentration (unless that is the IV)
SAFETY: Wear eye protection; acids and alkalis are irritant or corrosive; copper(II) sulfate is harmful.
Hydrogen released from metals with acid is flammable – keep away from flames; do not use metals more reactive than magnesium.
Do not use a glass thermometer to stir; do not heat the cup.
RESULTS: Neutralisation, metal + acid, displacement: temperature rises (exothermic). e.g. HCl + NaOH ≈ +13 °C; Zn + CuSO4 shows a larger rise than Fe + CuSO4 (more reactive metal displaces faster).
Citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate (or ammonium nitrate dissolving): temperature falls (endothermic).
With increasing concentration or amount (until a limiting reactant is used up) the temperature change increases, then levels off.
ANALYSIS: Temperature change ΔT = highest (or lowest) temperature – starting temperature.
Plot temperature against time (or ΔT against volume/concentration); extrapolate to find the maximum if heat loss affects the curve.
Mean of repeats; identify anomalies. Reaction is exothermic if the temperature rises; endothermic if it falls (only temperature change is required; no ΔH calculations).
ERRORS: Heat loss to the surroundings: lowers measured ΔT – use lid, insulation, polystyrene.
Heat absorbed by the cup/thermometer; solid not reacting fully; thermometer resolution; reaction too fast to record the maximum.
Improvements: use a lid, a polystyrene cup inside a beaker, a digital temperature probe with data logger, plot cooling correction, repeat and use means.
EXAM: State and justify control variables for a given experiment.
Explain the effect of insulation on the results; suggest improvements.
Identify exothermic/endothermic reactions from data; draw a graph and describe a trend.
Predict what would happen to ΔT if the concentration is doubled (until acid or alkali is the limiting reactant).

PURPOSE: To investigate how changes in concentration affect the rates of reactions by (a) a method involving measuring the volume of a gas produced and (b) a method involving a change in colour or turbidity, as an investigation involving developing a hypothesis.
APPARATUS: (a) Gas volume: conical flask, bung and delivery tube, gas syringe (or measuring cylinder inverted in water), stopwatch, hydrochloric acid of different concentrations (e.g. 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 mol/dm³), magnesium ribbon (same length) or marble chips

(b) Turbidity: dilute hydrochloric acid, sodium thiosulfate solution of different concentrations (made by diluting with water), conical flasks, measuring cylinders, a piece of paper with a black cross, stopwatch
Eye protection, safety lab coat
METHOD: (a) Measure a fixed volume of acid (e.g. 25 cm³) into the flask. Add a fixed length (e.g. 3 cm) of cleaned magnesium ribbon, immediately replace the bung and start the stopwatch. Record the volume of hydrogen in the gas syringe every 10 s for 2 minutes (or time to collect 30 cm³). Repeat with each concentration of acid.

(b) Place the flask on a black cross. Measure 50 cm³ of sodium thiosulfate solution of known concentration into the flask. Add 10 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid, start the stopwatch and swirl. Look down through the solution and stop the timer when the cross can no longer be seen. Repeat with solutions of different concentrations (changing thiosulfate concentration only, keeping total volume the same).
Repeat each concentration at least twice and calculate means.
IV: The concentration of the acid (a) or of the sodium thiosulfate solution (b).
DV: (a) The volume of gas produced per unit time (rate) or time to collect a fixed volume. (b) The time for the cross to disappear (rate = 1/time).
CV: Volume of solution(s) and amount/surface area of solid (mass or length and width of magnesium)
Temperature of the solutions (use a water bath)
Same observer and method for judging the end-point (b)
Total volume of liquid in (b)
SAFETY: Wear eye protection throughout; hydrochloric acid and sodium thiosulfate solution are irritant.

(b) The reaction produces sulfur dioxide, which is toxic and can trigger asthma: use dilute solutions, ventilated room, and dispose of mixtures promptly in a fume cupboard or according to instructions.
(a) Hydrogen is flammable; stopper loosely and keep flames away.
RESULTS: Higher concentration gives a faster rate: more gas produced in the same time (steeper curve) or a shorter time for the cross to disappear.
The graph of volume against time is steepest at the start and levels off when the limiting reactant is used up. Final volumes are the same if the same amount of limiting reactant is used.
Plot rate (or 1/t) against concentration: a straight line through the origin shows a proportional relationship.
ANALYSIS: Mean rate = volume of gas ÷ time (cm³/s). For (b), rate ∝ 1/time (e.g. 1/t in s⁻¹).
Draw tangents to volume–time graphs at t = 0 to compare initial rates; gradient = Δ volume ÷ Δ time (HT: calculate gradients).
Equations: Mg + 2HCl → MgCl2 + H2; Na2S2O3 + 2HCl → 2NaCl + S + SO2 + H2O.
Use collision theory to explain: higher concentration → more particles per unit volume → more frequent collisions → faster rate.
ERRORS: Delay between mixing and starting the stopwatch/bung; gas escaping before the bung is on.
Syringe sticking; bubbles in measuring cylinder; solutions of the wrong concentration.
(b) Judging when the cross disappears is subjective (use the same person, same light, same depth).
Magnesium ribbon surface oxide layer slows the start – clean with sandpaper.
Improvements: use a data logger/pressure sensor or balance, repeat and use means, use a colorimeter for (b).
EXAM: Write a hypothesis (e.g. 'As concentration doubles, the rate approximately doubles').
Explain how rate changes in terms of collisions.
Identify the dependent/independent/control variables; suggest improvements.
Describe how to measure rate from a graph (tangent, gradient).

PURPOSE: To investigate how paper chromatography can be used to separate and tell the difference between coloured substances (e.g. food colourings, inks) and to calculate Rf values.
APPARATUS: Chromatography paper (or filter paper) cut to size, pencil, ruler
Glass beaker or tank with lid (or cling film) as developing chamber
Capillary tubes or fine pipettes
Solvent (water, or ethanol/water mixtures)
Samples: several known food colourings or inks and an unknown mixture
Paper clip or splint and tape to hang the paper
METHOD: Draw a pencil line (the origin/baseline) about 1.5–2 cm from the bottom of the paper.
Put small spots (about 2 mm diameter) of each sample on the baseline, labelling each in pencil beneath; allow to dry and, if needed, add another drop on the same spot.
Pour a shallow layer of solvent into the beaker (depth less than 1 cm, below the baseline) and hang the paper in it so the bottom edge touches the solvent but the spots do not. Cover the beaker.
Allow the solvent to travel up the paper; remove it when the solvent front is close to the top and immediately mark the position of the solvent front with a pencil.
Dry the chromatogram. Measure from the baseline to the centre of each spot and to the solvent front.
DV: The distance moved by each colour (spot) and Rf values.
CV: Same type and size of paper
Same solvent and depth, same time of development
Same baseline height and spot size
Same temperature
SAFETY: Use pencil (not pen) for the baseline – ink would dissolve.
If ethanol or other flammable solvents are used, keep away from flames; ventilated area.
Wear eye protection; wash hands.
RESULTS: Mixtures separate into several spots; a pure substance gives a single spot.
Known colourings can be identified by matching the spots at the same height or the same Rf as the unknown.
Different solvents can change Rf values and the number of spots separated.
ANALYSIS: Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent (no units, always between 0 and 1).
Example: spot centre 4.2 cm from baseline; solvent front 7.0 cm: Rf = 4.2 ÷ 7.0 = 0.60.
Compare Rf values to data tables or the reference samples to identify substances; give answers to an appropriate number of significant figures.
ERRORS: Baseline under the solvent – the samples dissolve into the solvent.
Spots too large or too concentrated – overlapping, smearing; use small spots.
Not marking the solvent front immediately – inaccurate Rf.
Paper touching the beaker sides – uneven solvent front.
Measuring to different points on the spot – measure to the centre consistently.
Improvement: use a ruler and measure each spot twice, use a lid to keep the atmosphere saturated with solvent.
EXAM: Explain why a pencil line is used, why the baseline must be above the solvent, and why a lid is used.
Explain how chromatography separates the substances (stationary phase paper, mobile phase solvent, differences in solubility).
Calculate Rf; identify substances; decide whether a substance is pure.
Why might the same substance have different Rf values in different solvents?

PURPOSE: To use chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds, covering flame tests, metal hydroxide precipitates, carbonates, halides and sulfates.
APPARATUS: Nichrome (or platinum) wire loop, concentrated hydrochloric acid in a small beaker (or a splint soaked in solution), Bunsen burner
Solid and/or aqueous unknown samples (e.g. NaCl, KI, CuSO4, FeSO4, Na2CO3, CaCl2, MgSO4, Al(NO3)3)
Sodium hydroxide solution, dilute hydrochloric acid, dilute nitric acid, silver nitrate solution, barium chloride solution, limewater
Test tubes and rack, dropping pipettes, spatulas, distilled water, delivery tube with bung
Eye protection, lab coat, gloves where required
METHOD: Flame test: clean the wire loop by dipping in concentrated HCl and heating until no colour; dip it in the solid (moistened) or solution; hold in the edge of a non-luminous Bunsen flame and record the colour.

Metal hydroxides: dissolve a small amount of the unknown in distilled water; add sodium hydroxide solution a few drops at a time and record the precipitate colour; add excess to see whether a white precipitate dissolves.
Carbonates: add dilute hydrochloric acid to the solid or solution; if it fizzes, pass the gas through limewater and look for it turning milky.
Halides: add dilute nitric acid, then a few drops of silver nitrate solution; record the colour of the precipitate.
Sulfates: add dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution; look for a white precipitate.
Combine the results to identify the cation and the anion of each unknown, using the results table.
IV: The unknown ionic compound / the reagent used.
DV: Observed flame colour, precipitate colour or gas given off.
CV: Same volume of sample and number of drops of reagent
Clean equipment between tests
Same concentration of reagents
SAFETY: Wear eye protection; concentrated HCl is corrosive and must be handled carefully.
Barium chloride is toxic; silver nitrate stains skin and is harmful; nitric acid is corrosive; sodium hydroxide is corrosive.
Keep Bunsen flames away from flammable solvents; tie back hair.
RESULTS: Flame colours: Li⁺ crimson, Na⁺ yellow, K⁺ lilac, Ca²⁺ orange-red, Cu²⁺ green.
NaOH: Al³⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺ white precipitates (only Al(OH)3 dissolves in excess); Cu²⁺ blue; Fe²⁺ green; Fe³⁺ brown.
Carbonates fizz with acid and the gas turns limewater milky.
AgNO3/HNO3: Cl⁻ white, Br⁻ cream, I⁻ yellow precipitate.
BaCl2/HCl: SO4²⁻ white precipitate.
ANALYSIS: Deduce the ions in the unknown by combining results; write ionic equations, e.g. Cu²⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) → Cu(OH)2(s); Ag⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq) → AgCl(s); Ba²⁺(aq) + SO4²⁻(aq) → BaSO4(s).
To distinguish Ca²⁺ from Mg²⁺ (both white precipitates, insoluble in excess) use a flame test (calcium orange-red; magnesium no flame colour).
ERRORS: Contaminated wire or equipment gives wrong flame colours (sodium contamination turns flames yellow).
Judging subtle colours (e.g. cream vs white silver bromide, green vs blue precipitates).
Masking: mixtures of ions can hide flame colours.
Improvements: test known samples alongside; use fresh clean equipment; use white background; compare with controls.
EXAM: Describe how to carry out a given test and what a positive result looks like.
Identify an unknown compound from a table of results (name or formula).
Explain why dilute acid is added in the halide and sulfate tests (to remove carbonate/other ions that would give false positive precipitates).
Write ionic equations for the precipitation reactions.

PURPOSE: To analyse and purify water samples from different sources, including pH, dissolved solids and distillation.
APPARATUS: Water samples (e.g. sea water or salty water, rain water, tap water, polluted water; synthetic samples may be used)
pH meter or universal indicator and colour chart; or pH probe
Evaporating basin, balance, measuring cylinder (e.g. 10 or 25 cm³), Bunsen burner or water bath, tripod and gauze
Distillation apparatus: round-bottomed or conical flask, bung and delivery tube, condenser with water in at the bottom and out at the top, boiling chips, collecting flask
Eye protection, tongs, heat-proof mat
METHOD: pH: test each sample with a pH meter or universal indicator and record the pH.

Dissolved solids: weigh a clean, dry evaporating basin. Measure a known volume (e.g. 10 cm³) of the water sample into it. Evaporate gently over a water bath until only a dry solid remains (do not heat strongly). Cool and reweigh. The increase in mass is the mass of dissolved solids.
Distillation: heat a known volume of the water sample (add boiling chips) so that it boils gently and the steam passes through the condenser; collect the distillate. Stop before the flask boils dry.
Test the pH and dissolved solid content of the distillate to show purification.
IV: The source of the water sample (and whether it is distilled).
DV: pH, mass of dissolved solids per volume, and appearance of the distillate.
CV: Same volume of sample for each test
Same heating method/time for evaporation
Same equipment cleaned and dried
SAFETY: Wear eye protection; hot glassware and steam burns – use tongs and heat-proof mat.
Do not heat the evaporating basin to dryness over a naked flame (spitting); use a water bath for the last stage.
Do not seal the distillation apparatus (pressure build up); ensure water flows through the condenser from bottom to top.
Treat polluted samples as potentially hazardous; wash hands.
RESULTS: Tap water: pH about 7, small mass of dissolved solids. Sea water: pH about 8, large mass of solid left (salt). Rain water: pH slightly acidic (about 5–6), very few dissolved solids.
Distilled water: pH 7, no residue left on evaporation.
ANALYSIS: Concentration of dissolved solids = mass of solid (g) ÷ volume of water (dm³ or cm³), e.g. 0.35 g in 10 cm³ = 35 g/dm³.
Compare samples; relate pH to pollution (e.g. dissolved acidic gases such as sulfur dioxide) and dissolved solids to hardness/salinity.
Distillation separates pure water from dissolved solids based on boiling-point difference (simple distillation).
ERRORS: Spitting during evaporation loses solid; not drying completely gives a higher mass; hot basin on the balance causes errors.
Water may not all condense; low-volume samples give low precision; calibrate the pH meter.
Improvements: use larger volumes, heat to constant mass, weigh to 0.01 g, repeat and use mean.
EXAM: Distinguish potable and pure water; describe how to produce potable water.
Describe each stage of the experiment and why distillation is used.
Calculate the mass of dissolved solids; compare samples.
Explain safety precautions.

APPLY: Decimals in relative atomic and formula masses, moles and concentrations (4.3.1.2, 4.3.2, 4.3.4), rates of reaction (4.6.1.1), titration volumes (RP2) and Rf values (4.8.1.3, RP6).
Convert between cm³ and dm³ using decimals: 25.0 cm³ = 0.0250 dm³.
Standard form for size of atoms and nuclei (4.1.1.5: 1 × 10⁻¹⁰ m), the Avogadro constant 6.02 × 10²³ (4.3.2.1), nanoparticle and PM sizes (4.2.4.1).
Rule: A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10; negative n for numbers < 1.

Ratios, fractions and percentages: percentage by mass (4.3.1.2), mole ratios from balanced equations (4.3.2), percentage yield and atom economy (4.3.3), isotope abundance (4.1.1.6), surface area to volume ratios (4.2.4.1, 4.6.1.3), carat percentages (4.10.3.2), gas volume ratios (4.3.5), Rf (4.8.1.3), composition of air (4.9.1.1).
Estimating answers: check relative atomic mass lies between isotope masses (4.1.1.6); estimating sizes (4.1.1.5, 4.2.4.1) and orders of magnitude; estimating results in rate calculations (4.6.1.1).

Give answers to an appropriate number of significant figures – usually the same as the least precise value given: Rf values (4.8.1.3), moles and masses (4.3), percentage yield (4.3.3.1), concentration from titrations (RP2).
Arithmetic mean of repeats and concordant titres (RP2, RP4, RP5); use the range about the mean as uncertainty (4.3.1.4).
Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts and diagrams: resources data (4.10.1.1), temperature change charts (RP4), uncertainty distributions (4.3.1.4).

Order of magnitude: atom 10⁻¹⁰ m vs nucleus 10⁻¹⁴ m (4.1.1.5); nanoparticles vs fine/coarse particles (4.2.4.1); hydrogen ion concentration changes by factor of 10 per pH unit (4.4.2.6); evaluating resource data (4.10.1.1).
Symbols =, <, <<, >>, >, ∝, ~: rate ∝ 1/time (RP5), pH comparisons, approximate sizes (4.2.4.1), 'much greater than' for energy comparisons.
Change the subject of an equation: n = m ÷ Mr; c = n ÷ V; Rf = a ÷ b; % yield and atom economy; V = n × 24 (4.3.2, 4.3.3, 4.3.4, 4.3.5).
Substitute numerical values into algebraic equations using units: moles, concentration, gas volume, percentage yield, rate calculations. Always carry units (g, mol, dm³, cm³, s).
Translate information between graphical and numeric form: rate graphs (4.6.1.1), spectra (4.8.3.7), resources data (4.10.1.1), LCA data (4.10.2.1).
y = mx + c: a straight line through the origin shows direct proportionality (e.g. rate against concentration or 1/time against concentration, RP5).
Plot two variables from experimental data: independent variable on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis, labelled axes with units, sensible scale, points plotted accurately (RP4, RP5, 4.6.1.1).
Determine slope and intercept of a linear graph: gradient = Δy ÷ Δx (rate of reaction, 4.6.1.1); intercept gives initial values.
Draw and use the slope of a tangent to a curve as a measure of rate of change (4.6.1.1): rate of reaction at a point in time (HT calculation of gradient).

Visualise and represent 2D and 3D forms including two-dimensional representations of 3D objects: dot-and-cross diagrams, ball-and-stick, lattice diagrams, displayed formulae, carbon structures (4.2.1, 4.2.3, 4.7).
Areas of triangles and rectangles, surface areas and volumes of cubes: SA:V ratio of nanoparticles and rate of reaction (4.2.4.1, 4.6.1.3). Cube: SA = 6 × side², V = side³, SA:V = 6 ÷ side.

CALC: Relative atomic mass from isotopes: Ar = Σ(mass × % abundance) ÷ 100 (4.1.1.6).
Atom, ion subatomic particles: protons = atomic number; neutrons = mass number – atomic number; electrons = protons ± charge (4.1.1.5).
Relative formula mass Mr = sum of Ar; % by mass of element = (Ar × atoms ÷ Mr) × 100 (4.3.1.2).

UNIT CONVERSIONS: Volume: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³ = 1 litre; 1 cm³ = 0.001 dm³. Mass: 1 kg = 1000 g. Length: 1 nm = 1 × 10⁻⁹ m; 1 µm = 1 × 10⁻⁶ m; 1 mm = 1 × 10⁻³ m.
Concentration: g/dm³ = mol/dm³ × Mr. Molar volume of gas at room temperature and pressure = 24 dm³/mol = 24 000 cm³/mol.
STANDARD FORM: A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10. Multiply: add powers; divide: subtract powers. Use for atomic scales, Avogadro constant, nanoparticles.
SIGNIFICANT FIGURES: Count from the first non-zero digit. Give the final answer to the same number of s.f. as the least precise data given; do not round intermediate steps.
RATIOS AND PERCENTAGES: Mole ratios come from the large (balancing) numbers in equations; percentage = part ÷ whole × 100; percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100.
GRAPH INTERPRETATION: Gradient of a straight line = Δy ÷ Δx. On a rate graph (quantity vs time) the gradient is the rate. A plateau means a reactant has been used up.
Draw a tangent by placing a ruler at the point so the curve is equally either side; take a large triangle.
DATA ANALYSIS AND UNCERTAINTY: Concordant results (titrations) are within 0.10 cm³; exclude anomalies and rough titre.
Range = highest – lowest; uncertainty = ± range ÷ 2; repeatable, reproducible, accurate, precise definitions (WS 3.7).
Random errors lower with repeats and means; systematic errors shift all results by a similar amount.
